{'title': None, 'content': "There's an old saying in photography that the best camera is the one you have with you. The iPhone is, of course, the camera most of us have with us most of the time, which is a huge advantage for capturing scenes like kids or social events. But a recent video project made me notice another benefit."}

{'title': None, 'content': 'I really enjoy walking around London in the evening, and I often take photos and short videos with my iPhone. At first it was purely for my own enjoyment, but I later realised these clips could serve as B-roll footage for video projects…'}

{'title': None, 'content': "My current project is experimental in nature, designed to test the viability of Cinematic mode—which is why I lamented earlier that the company seems to have halted development on it. Once the project is complete, I'll share it with everyone next week."}

{'title': None, 'content': "This time I wanted to follow a very specific format, needing to cut in very short landscape B-roll paired with interview content. In theory, the footage could be shot anywhere in London, but since the main subject was filmed by the river, I really wanted all the B-roll to feature the Thames. I needed four clips, and I didn't have to search long in my iPhone videos before finding suitable footage."}

{'title': None, 'content': "The clip above also brings up another appealing aspect. When there are passersby in the frame who might be recognisable, I go up to them afterwards, show them the footage, and only seek their permission before using it. (This isn't a legal requirement in the UK, but I consider it a matter of courtesy.) Many of them proactively ask for a copy. If they also use iPhone, AirDrop can get it done quickly; for Android users, WhatsApp serves as a backup option."}

{'title': None, 'content': "The iPhone's stabilisation is truly excellent, especially for those unplanned, impromptu shots taken by hand while out on a walk. Although I do try to brace the phone against things like walls, railings or lamp posts to steady it, generally speaking the footage comes out very stable, arguably comparable to the results from a tripod. (If I've planned ahead for a walk-and-shoot session, I'll also bring a small GorillaPod tripod.)"}

{'title': None, 'content': "Another major advantage of the iPhone is its 'point-and-shoot' nature. If I had to manually set exposure, white balance, ND filters and so on, I'd probably find it too much hassle and not bother shooting, especially when walking with others—it would be too disruptive if it took too long. But asking someone to wait for just about 20 seconds or so doesn't really feel like it breaks the rhythm of the walk."}

{'title': None, 'content': 'If I want to stop somewhere for a while, shooting a time-lapse with the iPhone is also very straightforward. Once you start recording, you can stop at any time, and the iPhone automatically adjusts to give you a clip of suitable length. At my old flat, I used to prop my iPhone by the window, start a time-lapse at sunset, then carry on with my own things. A few of those clips later became excellent B-roll footage for video projects.'}

{'title': None, 'content': "Admittedly, if you zoom in pixel by pixel, the limitations of the iPhone's small sensor do start to show, especially in low-light conditions. But most YouTube viewers today watch on their phones or laptops, and for the vast majority of content the quality is already more than adequate."}

{'title': None, 'content': "Whether the same holds true for Cinematic mode footage, I'm less certain—you can all judge for me next week. But overall, having such a powerful camera constantly in my pocket, ready to use anytime, anywhere, really fills me with amazement."}
